name: Tonsure

lead: Tonsure is the cutting or shaving of some or all of the scalp hair, traditionally as a sign of religious devotion or humility. The word comes from the Latin tonsura, meaning clipping or shearing.[1]

As a look, the classic Roman form shaves only the top of the head and leaves a ring of hair, while Eastern traditions shave the whole head. Today it is mostly encountered as monastic practice or as a stylistic reference, since the purpose of religious tonsure is renunciation rather than fashion.[1]

paras: Historically a razor or scissors was used in a ceremony. Buddhist monastics keep the head shaved, with Theravada rules calling for shaving every two months or when hair reaches two finger-breadths.[1] Hair is a visible marker of religious identity rather than a grooming aid.

Deliberate tonsure carries no particular reported health risks beyond those of shaving the scalp. Separately, dermatology literature uses the term tonsure trichotillomania for a crown-focused pattern of hair loss caused by hair pulling.[2][3]

angle.text: Tonsure is a shaved-scalp style with strong religious meaning. Wearers outside religious settings who borrow the shaved-crown look use it as a stark, minimal hairstyle.

lead: Tonsure is the cutting or shaving of some or all of the scalp hair as a sign of religious devotion or humility. In medieval Catholicism it named a specific clerical rite, which the Church ended in 1972.[1]

Three Christian forms are described: the Oriental (whole head shaved), the Celtic (shaved from ear to ear, exact shape unclear) and the Roman (top shaved, leaving a crown of hair).[1] Catholic tradition linked the Roman form to Saint Peter, though the Wikipedia article notes no evidence for that.[1]

Tonsure also exists in Hinduism, where the chudakarana rite is a child's first haircut, and in Buddhism, where shaving is part of ordination.[1] For people interested in hair and looks, the term is chiefly a reference point for the shaved-crown silhouette. In dermatology the same word names a hair-loss pattern seen in trichotillomania.[2]

paras: No Christian tonsure records exist before the 6th century.[1] In 668 Theodore of Tarsus, who wore the Eastern tonsure, had to grow his hair out before Pope Vitalian ordained him Archbishop of Canterbury.[1] In the medieval period, first tonsure admitted men to the clergy; Pope Paul VI's Ministeria quaedam in 1972 stated that first tonsure is no longer conferred, though some groups were later authorised to use it again.[1]

In Hinduism, chudakarana is a child's first haircut, often done around the first birthday, and male mourners may shave their heads after a relative's death.[1] In Buddhism, tonsure is part of ordination and is repeated to keep the head shaved.[1] In Eastern Orthodoxy the practice today is a few locks cut in a cross shape.[1]

Dermatology uses "tonsure" to describe a crown pattern of hair loss. A 1995 German case report defines tonsure trichotillomania as alopecia over the crown extending to the frontal margin while sparing the sides and nape.[2] Other case reports and a 2014 trichoscopy study mention the same pattern in hair-pulling disorders.[3][4]
No studies found on tonsure as a hairstyle. Case reports and small studies of tonsure-pattern hair pulling (trichotillomania) exist.[2][3][4]
